name: MBR Performance
author: Robert Palmer
upgrade_notice: Minify CSS and Minify JavaScript now minify your stylesheet and script files; previously they had no effect. Also fixes quoted url() values being broken by the CSS minifier. Updating clears the page cache once.

sections.description: Full page caching plus granular, transparent WordPress performance optimisation across core, scripts, fonts, preloading, database, images, WooCommerce and multisite — including per-page and per-template Used CSS, and paste-in Critical CSS.
sections.changelog:
2.1.3

  • Fix: Minify CSS and Minify JavaScript did nothing. Both targeted inline blocks only, and even that never ran: the filters returned early for any handle with a src, and WordPress never calls them for a handle without one. The external files PageSpeed Insights lists under "Minify CSS" and "Minify JavaScript" were never touched, except inside a Combine CSS bundle.
  • New: each local stylesheet and script that is not already minified is served from a minified copy under /uploads/mbr-performance-min/, written on first request and rebuilt when the original changes. The copy mirrors the original path, so URL-fragment exclusions still match. .min files, files saving under 5%, external and excluded files, and scripts that locate themselves at run time (webpack chunks, workers) keep their original URL.
  • New: JavaScript is minified with a bundled tokeniser (JShrink, BSD licence) rather than pattern matching; a script it cannot parse is served unchanged. Combined JavaScript bundles are now minified too.
  • New: inline CSS and script attached to enqueued handles is minified.
  • Fix: the CSS minifier broke every quoted url() — url('font.woff2') reached the browser as a placeholder token, because a string token nested inside a url() token was never restored. This affected Combine CSS with minification on, and the CSS inlined by Used CSS and Mode B, so quoted font and background-image URLs inside them failed to load.
  • Fix: the CSS minifier joined a descendant combinator onto a following pseudo-class, turning ".menu :hover" into ".menu:hover".
  • Fix: saving or resetting settings deleted combined bundles but left the page cache holding pages that linked to them. Saving, resetting, or clearing the CSS or JS file cache now clears the page cache too.
  • Fix: Server and Diagnostics were missing from the toolbar menu. The menu and the tab row now share one list, and the menu is shown only to users who can manage options.
  • Updating clears the combined, Used CSS, Mode B and page caches once.

2.1.2

  • Fix: with page caching enabled, Used CSS never took effect. The page cache stored the first render of each page, served untouched while its used CSS was generated, and every later visitor was served that stored copy without reaching PHP. The same applied to Mode B while learning. Generating and learning renders are now served but not stored, so the optimised page is what gets cached.
  • Fix: the page cache now clears its entry for a URL when Used CSS or Mode B finishes it.
  • Fix: Used CSS and Mode B analysed the wrong HTML when HTML minify or the Google Fonts strip were on, and discarded their processing for that request. They now capture their own buffer and analyse after every buffer has been flushed.
  • Fix: pages with nothing for Used CSS to optimise are no longer re-analysed on every request, and are page-cached normally.
  • Updating clears the page cache once.

2.1.1

  • Fix: the OPcache panel said OPcache was switched off on servers running it in file-cache-only mode, the standard configuration on SiteGround and some other managed hosts. PHP marks the shared-memory cache as disabled in that mode, and 2.1.0 read that as OPcache being off. "Switched off" is now reported only when opcache.enable itself is 0.
  • New: file-cache mode is recognised and explained, showing the mode, whether PHP checks for changed files, and whether the plugin's own files are refreshed on write.
  • Fix: Flush OPcache is no longer offered in file-cache mode, where opcache_reset() leaves the disk cache untouched. The plugin's own files are still invalidated individually.
  • Fix: a host that runs OPcache but hides its status from plugins is reported as exactly that, not as OPcache being off.
  • Fix: the opcache.restrict_api check compares against the requested script, as PHP does.

2.1.0

  • New: OPcache panel on the Diagnostics tab — hit rate, memory used, wasted and free, cached files against the server's file-slot limit, restart counts, whether PHP checks for changed files, and when OPcache last restarted.
  • New: plain-English findings when OPcache is not installed, switched off, restricted by the host, short of memory or file slots, or holding a large share of outdated copies, naming the php.ini setting to ask the host about. OPcache is configured at server level, so the plugin reports and flushes rather than offering switches it cannot provide.
  • New: Flush OPcache, on the Diagnostics tab and in the toolbar menu. Requires manage_options, or super admin on multisite, where a flush affects every site on the server.
  • Fix: advanced-cache.php and wp-config.php are now invalidated in OPcache as soon as the plugin writes them, as the cache config already was. On hosts with validate_timestamps off, a refreshed drop-in or a WP_CACHE change previously sat on disk unused until OPcache was next flushed.
  • New: on WordPress older than 6.2, plugins, themes and translations updated through WordPress are invalidated in OPcache afterwards, and a core update flushes it. 6.2 and newer do this themselves.
  • New: mbrpe_opcache_reset action, fired after every flush attempt.
  • Fix: the Server tab could not switch its rules off with both boxes unticked, because the browser sent nothing for the section and the saved values were kept.

2.0.2

  • Fix: pages served by the static (.htaccess) cache tier were sent with X-Robots-Tag: noindex. The guard .htaccess written into the cache directory set that header on every .html and .gz file in the folder, intending to stop search engines indexing the raw cache files if they were browsed directly. Directory rules apply to every response served from that folder, including the cache hits the root rewrite rules send there, so every HIT-STATIC page told search engines not to index it. Drop-in hits and cache misses were unaffected.
  • Fix: the guard .htaccess now refuses direct requests for the cache path with a 403 instead, matching on the original request line so rewritten cache hits pass untouched.
  • Fix: plain (non-gzipped) static cache hits are now sent with charset=UTF-8. Previously only the pre-compressed copies declared one.
  • Fix: the guard file is versioned and rewritten when out of date. It was previously written only if missing, and purging deliberately preserves it, so a faulty guard could never be replaced. Updating rewrites it immediately and existing cached pages are corrected without a purge.
  • Note: if a search engine has already dropped pages because of this, request re-indexing once the update is installed.

2.0.1

  • Security: pasted Critical CSS is stripped of tag fragments repeatedly rather than in a single pass. A single pass could be defeated by a crafted string whose removal rejoined its neighbours into a working </style>, letting anyone able to save plugin settings place arbitrary JavaScript on the front end. On multisite that crossed a real boundary, because site Administrators do not hold unfiltered_html.
  • Security: the Optimise, Repair and Convert to InnoDB tools now act only on the current site's own tables. They previously enumerated every table the database user could see — on a multisite network, every other site's tables; on shared-database hosting, potentially a neighbouring install. A Super Admin on the main site still gets the network-shared tables. Failures now report the table name rather than the raw database error.
  • Security: the RUM beacon is rate-limited per client and capped on total stored rows. The previous limit was keyed on the request path, which the caller chooses, so rotating it left an unauthenticated endpoint writing a row per request.
  • Security: media deletion resolves sub-size filenames with basename() and confirms every file sits inside the uploads directory before removing it, rather than trusting the path components in attachment metadata.
  • Security: the stylesheet and script combiners check file extensions before reading. Resolving inside the WordPress directory was previously sufficient, and the result is published under wp-content/uploads.
  • Security: downloaded font files must come from fonts.gstatic.com over HTTPS, and font family names are URL-encoded before being placed in the API request.
  • Fix: the cache key's scheme and host are now derived identically by the plugin and by the advanced-cache.php drop-in. The two had drifted — the drop-in trusted X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-SSL unconditionally while the plugin used is_ssl() — so on a site not behind a proxy a forged header sent the reader to a branch the writer never populated, costing a permanent cache miss for those requests. The scheme is now pinned from home_url(); forwarded headers are consulted only when the new trust_proxy config flag is set.
  • Fix: the Host header is validated as a hostname and, on single-site installs, checked against the hosts the site actually answers to. It was previously character-stripped and used as-is, so varying the header alone created unlimited cache directories. Domain aliases can be added with the new mbrpe_cache_hosts filter.
  • Fix: Google Fonts with capitalised names now download. Family names were forced to Title Case before the request, turning "IBM Plex Sans" into "Ibm Plex Sans" — a name Google answers with a 400, so the download failed with no explanation. The name is now sent as you typed it, and an all-lower-case name is retried in Title Case so "open sans" still works. This affected every family with an acronym in it, including IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, DM Sans, PT Serif and EB Garamond.
  • Fix: a font that fails to download is no longer recorded as installed, which previously left the front end requesting a stylesheet that was never written. Failures now explain that family names are case-sensitive and that the weight must be one the family publishes.
  • Fix: enabling Google Fonts self-hosting or removal no longer takes unrelated theme CSS with it. Matching stylesheets were deregistered as well as dequeued, and WordPress silently refuses to print any stylesheet that named the removed handle as a dependency, along with any inline CSS attached to it — Customizer colour rules such as a semi-transparent header background included. The handle is now kept and its source blanked. The same change applies to the Font Awesome removal option.
  • Fix: the Disable Dashicons option no longer deregisters the dashicons handle, only stops it loading. Themes and plugins commonly enqueue their own stylesheet with dashicons as a dependency, and deregistering it meant WordPress silently declined to print those stylesheets. The option applies to logged-out visitors only, so it would not have been visible while logged in.
  • Fix: removing Google Fonts resource hints no longer removes every other resource hint on the page.
  • Hardening: admin notices render server-supplied messages as text rather than markup; directory containment checks compare with a trailing separator; the bundled autoloader refuses traversal sequences in a class name.
  • Upgrade note: the drop-in contract version is raised to 2.0.1. Updating refreshes the installed drop-in, rewrites the cache config and clears existing cached pages once, because entries written before this release were keyed the old way. Your settings, including whether caching is on, are unchanged.

2.0.0

  • New: full page caching. The finished HTML of each page is written to disk and served to subsequent visitors instead of being rebuilt. Three serving tiers, fastest first: optional .htaccess rules that let Apache or LiteSpeed answer a hit with no PHP at all; an advanced-cache.php drop-in that starts PHP but not WordPress, which works on every host including Nginx; and an in-WordPress fallback for locked-down filesystems. Off by default.
  • New: targeted purging. Editing a post clears that post, the front page, the blog index, every term across every taxonomy, the post type archive, the author archive, the date archives and the adjacent posts — not the whole cache. Comments, term edits, profile changes and WooCommerce stock movements each purge only what they affect.
  • New: X-MBR-Cache debug headers reporting HIT, MISS or BYPASS, with a bypass naming the specific rule responsible.
  • New: query-string normalisation — around twenty analytics and ad-click parameters are stripped before lookup, so a link shared with ?utm_source= serves the same entry as the clean URL.
  • New: pre-compressed gzip copies written alongside each cached page.
  • New: Cache tab with a status panel reporting the active serving tier, cached page count, WP_CACHE and drop-in state and directory writability, with a repair button beside anything wrong. Purge controls added to the admin toolbar.
  • Safety: logged-in visitors are never served from cache, and no page emitting a Set-Cookie header is ever stored. Password-protected posts, previews, search, the WooCommerce cart, checkout and account pages, and any request carrying a login, comment, password or cart cookie are excluded by default.
  • Safety: only complete HTML documents are stored, so a fatal error mid-render cannot be frozen into the cache. Files are written to a temporary name and renamed into place atomically.
  • Safety: page caching refuses to run while another page cache is active, naming the plugin responsible. wp-config.php and .htaccess are backed up before first modification, and the edited wp-config.php is syntax-checked before being written.
  • Change: the cache buffer wraps every other MBR optimisation, so minified HTML and Used CSS Mode B output are baked into the cached file — those modules then cost nothing on a cache hit.
  • Change: deactivating removes the drop-in, the rewrite rules and every cached file.
  • Upgrade note: page caching is switched off after upgrading. Enable it on the Cache tab when you are ready.

1.23.1

  • Fix: activation and deactivation now actually run. The hooks were registered against the bootstrap file rather than the main plugin file, so WordPress never fired them — a fresh install created none of its database tables and scheduled no cron jobs, and deactivating left .htaccess blocks and caches behind. Existing installs are repaired automatically on upgrade.
  • Fix: WebP/AVIF .htaccess delivery now works when WordPress is installed in a subdirectory, where the rewrite condition previously never matched and every visitor silently received the original JPEG. If you had this enabled on a subdirectory site, toggle it off and on to write the corrected rules.
  • Fix: images could be wrapped in a <picture> element twice, producing nested markup, because more than one filter can see the same image. Wrapping is now idempotent and existing <picture> elements are left alone. The Gutenberg block filter also gained the context guard the other filters already had.
  • Fix: PHP 7.4 compatibility. The bundled Symfony CssSelector calls str_contains(), which is PHP 8.0+, and would fatal on 7.4 during a Used CSS analysis. Symfony's own polyfill dependency had not been vendored alongside it; it now is.
  • Security: TLS certificate verification is no longer disabled on outbound requests. The Google Fonts downloader writes its responses into the uploads directory, so those now verify with no fallback; requests to the site's own front end verify by default and fall back only for the site's own host, so self-signed staging certificates keep working.
  • Security: the bulk WebP/AVIF converters now resolve the submitted path and confirm it lands inside the uploads directory and is a supported image. Both endpoints already required a nonce and manage_options; this is defence in depth.
  • New: uninstall.php. Deleting the plugin removes its options, tables, scheduled events, transients and caches. Your Media Library is untouched, and generated WebP/AVIF files and self-hosted fonts are left in place since a cache or CDN may still reference them.
  • Housekeeping: removed three unreferenced JavaScript files and an obsolete bundled copy of the Plugin Update Checker (v5.6).

1.23.0

  • New: Used CSS Mode B — per-template critical CSS that genuinely removes the unused stylesheets rather than deferring them, so the bytes stop being downloaded at all. One cache entry per template instead of one per page. Off by default.
  • New: multi-sample template learning. Each template is learned from several distinct URLs and keeps the union of what they used, so a rule only one page needs still survives for the whole template. Learning visits are served untouched.
  • New: selector safelist — the guard rail for anything JavaScript adds after load (consent banners, cart drawers, modals, scroll-toggled classes), which a static analysis cannot see.
  • Safety: a stylesheet is only removed if that exact file was analysed while learning. Sheets carrying @import, print and narrow-media sheets, external sheets and excluded sheets are always left alone.
  • Safety: the inlined CSS replaces the first stylesheet it stands in for, preserving the original cascade position; media="screen" rules are re-wrapped so they cannot leak into print.
  • Change: Mode A, Async CSS and Combine CSS all stand down when Mode B is on — the modes are alternatives. Hand-pasted Critical CSS still takes precedence over both.
  • New: the Performance Doctor understands both modes, recommends one or the other but never both, and reports whether Mode B is working, still learning, or leaving sheets alone by design.
  • New: ?mbrpe_modeb=off serves a single request with its original stylesheets, for comparing against the optimised page.

1.22.1

  • New: the Performance Doctor now understands script modules — it counts them, reports where the import map and preload hints landed, and recommends preload hoisting when it would help.
  • New: import map ordering check. A module printed in the head while the map sits in the footer cannot resolve its bare specifier imports; the Doctor now flags this as high priority.
  • New: the Doctor tells apart hoisting off, hoisting still learning the URL, and hoisting working — and tells block themes plainly that core already handles it.
  • Note: the learned module map is keyed on plugin version, so this upgrade clears it by design. Hoisted hints resume from the second visit to each URL.

1.22.0

  • New: Script Modules and Interactivity API support (WP 6.5+), including module preload hoisting that fixes late preload hints on classic themes.
  • New: static dependency graph walking, fetchpriority control, preload cap and exclusions. Off by default.

1.21.3

  • Fix: PDF report preview now renders as a centred A4 sheet instead of stretching to the browser width.
  • Fix: Note badge styling in reports; proper tab names on recommendation links.

1.21.2

  • Fix: real-user field data now appears in the Doctor site-scan view (it was being stripped by the info-tier roll-up filter).
  • Change: field data reported once site-wide rather than per template, and provisional notes now show the actual readings.

1.21.1

  • Fix: RUM field data now reaches the Performance Doctor immediately via on-demand aggregation, rather than waiting for the nightly cron.
  • New: "Run aggregation now" button; clearer status reporting; provisional p75s shown from 10 samples.

1.21.0

  • New: self-hosted Real User Monitoring — collects real-user Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP) into local tables and shows field data per template and per URL. No cookies, no IPs, nothing leaves your server. Off by default.
  • Hardening: the plugin's own mbrpe/v1 REST namespace is always permitted through REST hardening so the RUM beacon works for logged-out visitors.

1.20.1

  • Update checks now served from GitHub for reliable delivery.
  • Consolidated self-hosted release; corrected update manifest.
sections.installation: Upload the plugin to /wp-content/plugins/, activate, and configure under MBR → Performance.
